title: ReplicateBE.jl reproduces SAS Method C exactly on the fully replicate design and not on the partial replicate one
raised_by: PR #61, testing the ReplicateBE.jl Satterthwaite claim
effect_on_be_stats: DECISIVE, and in both directions. PR #62 implemented Appendix C for FULLY REPLICATE designs only, and this finding is the entire reason for that boundary: the oracle is verified for 2x2x4 and unverified for 2x3x3, so the fully replicate case has something to be checked against and the partial replicate case does not. FDA_REPLICATE_STANDARD_ABE_FULL is IMPLEMENTED_UNVALIDATED; FDA_REPLICATE_STANDARD_ABE_PARTIAL is NOT_IMPLEMENTED and refuses with APPENDIX_C_PARTIAL_REPLICATE_NOT_VALIDATED. Neither 19.603 nor 22.540 appears as a constant anywhere in the package, and an AST test enforces that.

oracle.name: ReplicateBE.jl
oracle.role: external oracle only; never a dependency of be_stats, never copied into it

data_set_i.reading: Every published quantity reproduces at the precision EMA printed. The CI is the load-bearing one: it is a function of the estimate, the SE AND the df, so matching it to two decimals means the df matches too. That is the Satterthwaite denominator df - the quantity with no other oracle - confirmed indirectly but tightly, on the UNBALANCED data set with incomplete subjects.

boundary_solution.note: Exactly 1.000 - a boundary solution. sigma2_D = sigma2_BT + sigma2_BR - 2*rho*sqrt(sigma2_BT*sigma2_BR) collapses to (sqrt(sigma2_BT) - sqrt(sigma2_BR))^2 there, i.e. no subject-by-formulation interaction beyond a scale difference. SAS's FA0(2) is likewise constrained to the positive-semidefinite boundary and would reach the same edge.
boundary_solution.consequence_for_a_future_implementation: The optimum for REAL data can sit on the boundary of the parameter space. An implementation that assumes an interior optimum, or inverts a Hessian without checking, will fail on exactly the data set that otherwise validates it.

data_set_ii.reading: The estimate and the covariance parameters match; the interval does not. It is narrower than published by about 0.035 percentage points at each end, roughly seven times the rounding bound. The whole difference is in the df: with SE = 0.030317 - a value nlme, glmmTMB and ReplicateBE.jl all agree on exactly - the published interval requires t = 1.72643, i.e. df about 19.60, against ReplicateBE's 22.540.

run_to_run_reproducibility.observed: Two identical CI runs gave df 22.540251 and 22.529500 for Data set II - a difference of 0.0108, about 0.05%. Data set I gave 208.081147 both times, identical.
run_to_run_reproducibility.cause: REML optimiser tolerance. Data set I's fit sits on the correlation boundary (rho = 1.000 exactly), which pins it; Data set II's optimum is interior (rho = 0.966) and flatter, so the search terminates at slightly different points.
run_to_run_reproducibility.consequence_for_the_ci: None visible. Both runs give the same 90% CI to four decimal places, because a 0.05% change in df moves t(0.95, 22.5) by about 1e-5.
run_to_run_reproducibility.consequence_for_a_future_validation: A tolerance on df in any future tier-3 case must accommodate the ORACLE'S OWN run-to-run variation, not just the difference between implementations. Roughly 0.02 df is the floor here; a tolerance tighter than that would fail against the oracle at random.
run_to_run_reproducibility.why_it_is_recorded: It would otherwise be discovered as a mysterious intermittent failure months later, which is exactly how VAL-FDA-HVD-001 started.

explanation.the_packages_own_scope: Satterthwaite degree of freedom (DF) estimate is equal with SAS/SPSS DF estimate for full-replicated basic bioequivalence balanced and unbalanced datasets (2x2x4, 2x2x3)
explanation.reading: Both named designs are TWO-SEQUENCE designs. Data set I is 2x2x4 and is covered. Data set II is a THREE-SEQUENCE partial replicate and is not. The observed pattern is exactly what the package claims - agreement where it says so, divergence where it never claimed any. A scope limitation honestly stated by its author, not a defect discovered here.

why: Three implementations agree the SE is 0.030317, which makes df about 19.60 the value consistent with SAS's published interval.
But all three could share a difference from SAS that only surfaces in this design.
Resolving it needs a SAS run - the same shortest path VAL-FDA-APPENDIX-C-001 already identifies.
what_is_not_established.nothing_was_tuned: The recovered 19.60 is a diagnostic. SAS's actual df for this design remains unpublished, and no parameter was adjusted toward it.

consequence: The oracle is VERIFIED for fully replicate (2x2x4) and UNVERIFIED for partial replicate (2x3x3). FDA HVD supports both designs, so this is not enough to implement Appendix C for BOTH - which is what PR #61 concluded when it recorded VAL-FDA-APPENDIX-C-001 as BLOCKED_WITH_PRECISE_REASONS. PR #62 took the other available route: implement the half the oracle covers and refuse the half it does not, rather than implementing neither or implementing both on one design's evidence.

superseded_in_part_by.what_changed: The conclusion 'not enough to implement Appendix C against' was correct about implementing it for BOTH designs and too strong about the fully replicate case, where the evidence was always sufficient. The scope split is the resolution.
superseded_in_part_by.what_did_not_change: Everything about the partial replicate design. The correct partial replicate Satterthwaite df remains NOT DETERMINED, and resolving it still needs a SAS run.
